The Swan mussel Anodonta cygnea, a large freshwater bivalve widely distributed across European still-water habitats, exhibits several distinctive life-history traits that have been characterised through long-term field studies and laboratory observations. The maximum reported shell length for this species approaches 20 centimetres [Li = 20 centimetres], a size that places it among the larger unionid mussels in the Palearctic region. Newly released glochidia, the parasitic larvae that attach to fish hosts, have an estimated wet weight at birth of approximately 0.000007 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000007 grams], a remarkably modest initial mass that reflects the tiny dimensions of these larval stages, which typically measure between 306 and 309 micrometres in length. This minute body size at the onset of the parasitic phase imposes a significant challenge for the larvae, as they must locate a suitable fish host within a short window of viability after release from the maternal gill. Field surveys conducted in temperate lowland lakes have documented that the species can attain a shell length of over 15 centimetres within roughly eight to ten years, although growth rates vary considerably with local productivity and water temperature regimes.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 16.5 °C [T = 16.5 °C], researchers have determined that the maximum reproductive output of Anodonta cygnea reaches approximately 7000 glochidia released per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 7000 glochidia released per spawning event], with a single spawning event occurring each year [F_R_i = single spawning event occurring each year]. This reproductive output is among the highest recorded for European unionid mussels, reflecting an r-selected strategy that compensates for the high mortality experienced during the parasitic larval stage. Gravid females brooding developing glochidia in their marsupial gills can be identified by the visibly swollen and distended appearance of the outer demibranchs during late spring and early summer. The timing of glochidial release is closely synchronised with the activity patterns of potential fish hosts, primarily benthic-feeding cyprinids such as roach and rudd, which are most abundant in shallow littoral zones during the warm months. Estimates of annual fecundity derived from these release patterns suggest that a single large female may produce several million glochidia over the course of a single reproductive season, although the actual number that successfully attach to a host and complete metamorphosis into juvenile mussels is exceedingly small.

Longevity records for Anodonta cygnea, based on mark-recapture studies and shell annulus analysis, indicate that individuals can survive for approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years] when maintained under stable thermal conditions at 16.5 °C [T = 16.5 °C], though maximum lifespan in natural populations may be somewhat shorter owing to predation, parasitism, and habitat degradation. This lifespan is intermediate among European unionids, falling between the shorter-lived species such as Anodonta anatina, which rarely exceeds eight years, and the longer-lived Margaritifera margaritifera, which can persist for over a century. The shell growth rings, formed annually during periods of reduced metabolic activity in winter, provide a reliable ageing method for this species, with each distinct ring representing a year of somatic growth. Growth is most rapid during the first three to five years of life, after which the rate of increase in shell length slows considerably as resources are increasingly diverted toward reproductive effort. The attainment of such a lifespan requires that individuals maintain physiological function across multiple reproductive seasons, a feat that is facilitated by the species' relatively low metabolic demands and its ability to filter-feed efficiently on suspended phytoplankton and detritus.

The onset of reproductive maturity in Anodonta cygnea, defined as the age at which individuals first develop functional gonads and begin gametogenesis, occurs at approximately 730 days after birth [tp = approximately 730 days after birth] when reared at a constant water temperature of 16.5 °C [T = 16.5 °C]. This relatively short pre-reproductive period, spanning roughly two years, is characteristic of many anodontine species and allows for rapid population turnover in productive habitats. Histological examination of gonad tissue from laboratory-reared individuals has confirmed that both males and females become capable of producing mature gametes by the end of their second growing season, with spermatogenesis typically preceding oogenesis by several weeks. The onset of puberty is closely linked to the attainment of a minimum body size rather than a strict age threshold, as individuals that experience slower growth rates may not reach reproductive competence until their third or fourth year. This size-dependent maturation schedule provides a degree of flexibility that buffers populations against year-to-year variation in food availability and thermal conditions. Field populations in nutrient-rich lakes often show earlier maturation than those in oligotrophic waters, reflecting the influence of local resource availability on developmental rates.

Comparative ecophysiological studies of freshwater bivalves have highlighted several parameters that distinguish Anodonta cygnea from its congeners, particularly with respect to the interplay between body size, reproductive output, and longevity. The maximum shell length of 20 centimetres [Li = 20 centimetres] recorded for this species is matched only by a few other European unionids, such as the closely related Anodonta anatina, though the latter typically reaches a more modest adult size under similar environmental conditions. The minute birth mass of 0.000007 grams [Wwb = 0.000007 grams] for newly released glochidia represents a common pattern among parasitic unionid larvae, which must balance the energetic costs of yolk provision against the need to produce large numbers of offspring. Longevity data from the same cohort of individuals used to estimate the 12-year lifespan (12 years) [am = 12 years] at 16.5 °C [T = 16.5 °C] also provided essential information on the duration of the reproductive window, with females remaining gravid for most of their adult life once puberty is attained at 730 days after birth [tp = 730 days after birth] under the same thermal regime. These integrated life-history traits collectively define a slow-paced, energetically conservative reproductive strategy that is well suited to the stable, low-disturbance lake environments the species typically inhabits.
